meilah-7a-10-11.note: Rabbi Shimon told how, in the village of Pani, an old man asked him whether Rabbi Akiva really said that sprinkling the blood takes effect for sacrificial meat that has left the courtyard, and he answered yes. His colleagues in the Galilee objected: the meat is unfit, so how can the sprinkling work for it? When he brought this to Rabbi Akiva, Akiva said: my son, don't you agree? He pointed to two sin offerings, a lost one and its replacement, where sprinkling the blood of one frees the other's meat from the laws of misuse even though that other animal is unfit; all the more should the blood free its own meat.
meilah-7a-10-11.why: Rabbi Akiva's comparison was cited and then limited by Rabbi Elazar to two animals slaughtered at once; right after this account, Reish Lakish says Akiva gave his student a misleading answer.

meilah-17a-9-14.note: In Rome, Rabbi Matya ben Ḥarash asked Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai how we know creeping animals' blood is impure, and got a verse. He told his admiring students it was Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yosei's tradition, and told why: Rome had forbidden Shabbat and circumcision. Rabbi Reuven ben Isterobeli, passing as a gentile, talked them out of each decree, but once they saw he was a Jew they restored them. The Sages sent Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai with Rabbi Elazar. On the road Rabbi Elazar whispered that verse in his teacher's presence, and Rabbi Shimon cursed him never to return to his father. The demon ben Temalyon possessed the emperor's daughter; Rabbi Shimon drove it out, and in the emperor's treasury they found the decree and tore it up.
meilah-17a-9-14.why: The Gemara has been discussing when blood joins with flesh to make up a measure for impurity. The story is attached because it records where the teaching that creeping animals' blood is impure comes from.
